shows: Mandiant reports that a Sandworm intrusion at a Ukrainian critical infrastructure organization began on, or prior to, June 2022 and culminated in two disruptive events on 10 and 12 October 2022. With the initial access vector into the IT environment unidentified, Sandworm reached the OT environment through a hypervisor hosting a SCADA management instance for the victim's substation environment; based on evidence of lateral movement, the attacker potentially had access to the SCADA system for up to three months. The October OT event resulted in an unscheduled power outage. Two days after the OT event, Sandworm deployed a new CADDYWIPER variant in the victim's IT environment to cause further disruption and potentially remove forensic artifacts; the wiper was limited to the IT environment and did not impact the hypervisor or the SCADA virtual machine. Mandiant notes that the disruptive capability was potentially developed as early as three weeks before the OT event, suggesting the attacker may have been waiting for a specific moment to deploy it.
limits: One incident at one organization, reconstructed by the vendor that responded to it, with stated uncertainty: SCADA access was 'potentially' up to three months, the executed commands were not recovered, and the initial access vector into the IT environment was not identified, so the report does not show how access was obtained and reports no credential theft. No outage duration, customers or area affected, restoration time or economic loss is reported. The two-day interval is between calendar dates (10 and 12 October 2022); no clock time is given for the OT event, so 48 hours is a day-count conversion, not a measured interval. The follow-on was an IT wiper, not a second OT action, and Mandiant suggests a possible lack of coordination between operational subteams; the report does not show that OT access was retained or used after the outage. The timing overlapped Russian kinetic operations, but Mandiant lacks sufficient evidence to assess a link. An access window in one grid intrusion is not a dwell-time distribution and does not transfer to other utilities, pharmaceutical IT or emergency-management systems without an explicit argument.

followon_delay_h.note: Derived: the report dates the OT event 10 October and the IT wiper 12 October 2022 ('Two days after the OT event'); 2 days x 24 h per day. No clock time is given for the OT event, so this is a calendar-day interval, not a measured one.

locator: ATT&CK for ICS technique T0832 page, ATT&CK content v19.2 (technique version 1.0, last modified 15 April 2025): description; Procedure Examples rows S0604 Industroyer; S0603 Stuxnet
shows: MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique T0832 Manipulation of View (technique version 1.0, last modified 15 April 2025): 'Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the information reported back to operators or controllers', so that 'the process itself could be in a much different state than what is reported', and 'operators may issue inappropriate control sequences that introduce faults or catastrophic failures into the system.' The page lists two procedure examples, both quoted: Industroyer's OPC module sends a status that 'equates to a Primary Variable Out of Limits misdirecting operators from understanding protective relay status', and 'Stuxnet manipulates the view of operators replaying process input and manipulating the I/O image to evade detection and inhibit protection functions.' Neither example targets emergency-responder, dispatch or coordination records.
limits: A technique entry documents an adversary behaviour class and named procedure examples, which MITRE summarises from the reports it cites. It does not establish success, reach, timing or consequence in any scenario, and a catalogue cannot establish that no other incident exists. Neither listed example involves a safety instrumented system or Triton, so this page does not support attributing operator-view manipulation to a Triton-class attack.

quotes.text: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the information reported back to operators or controllers. This manipulation may be short term or sustained. During this time the process itself could be in a much different state than what is reported.
With a manipulated view into the systems, operators may issue inappropriate control sequences that introduce faults or catastrophic failures into the system.

Industroyer's OPC module can brute force values and will send out a 0x01 status which for the target systems equates to a Primary Variable Out of Limits misdirecting operators from understanding protective relay status.
Stuxnet manipulates the view of operators replaying process input and manipulating the I/O image to evade detection and inhibit protection functions.

shows: In a press release of October 10, 2024 filed with the SEC as Exhibit 99.1 to a Form 8-K, American Water, the largest regulated US water and wastewater utility company (more than 14 million people served in 14 states), stated that it was methodically reconnecting and reactivating the systems it had taken offline after the cybersecurity incident it had announced on October 7. It continued to have no indication that its water and wastewater facilities were impacted, and the incident did not affect water quality. The disruption fell on business systems: the MyWater customer portal was back in operation and standard billing was resuming after a short period when the customer and billing platform was unavailable, with no late charges for that period. The investigation with law enforcement was ongoing.
limits: A company statement during an open investigation; it does not describe the attack, the systems taken offline, or how operational and business networks were separated, and 'no indication' is not proof of no effect. It shows that a large utility's business systems can be disrupted for days without any reported loss of water service, not that operational systems are immune.

locator: Product page sections 'What GAO Found' and 'Why GAO Did This Study'
shows: GAO's product page for its May 21, 2026 testimony before the House Science, Space, and Technology Subcommittee on the Environment summarises the cybersecurity of the close to 170,000 US water and wastewater systems. It states that in 2024 GAO found EPA had not performed key cybersecurity risk management steps for the sector and made recommendations, and that in response EPA conducted a water sector risk assessment and developed a risk management plan to guide its efforts to mitigate priority risks. In response to GAO's recommendation to evaluate its legal authorities, EPA identified critical gaps: no cybersecurity risk assessment requirements for wastewater systems and certain drinking water systems, and significant limitations in its authority under federal drinking water and clean water laws to address those gaps, which GAO will continue to monitor. The page also notes workforce shortages, older technology that is hard to protect, and competing financial priorities at utilities. The statement draws on GAO's August 2024 report GAO-24-106744, EPA documents and public information as of May 2026.
limits: A summary page, not the testimony itself, and it does not date EPA's risk assessment and plan (the specification's 'January 2025' does not appear in the retrieved text). It describes governance gaps and sector vulnerability, not incident counts, outage durations or consequences, and the 170,000 figure covers all water and wastewater systems, not community water systems alone.

valid_for.population: close to 170,000 US water and wastewater systems and EPA as sector risk management agency

It produces and distributes approximately 1.2 billion gallons of drinking water a year from separate and redundant groundwater and surface-water sources, and delivers it through numerous pump stations and over 180 miles of pipe into a series of reservoirs that feed thousands of hydrants and service connections. locator: Abstract (manuscript lines 7-19); Section 3.3 Restoration plan (lines 228-264); Section 3.7 restoration module (lines 400-415); Section 5 Los Angeles case study (lines 496-555, 585-596)
shows: Naeimi and Davidson present REWET, an open-source Python model of water system functioning and restoration after a damaging event. It couples pressure-demand driven hydraulic analysis (EPANET 2.2 with enhancements) to a discrete event simulation of the restoration process. The user defines, for each damaged element type, the actions that must be done and their order (for example inspect, isolate, reroute, repair), zones, one or more crew types with shifts (for example a daytime shift of 8 am to 8 pm) and reporting locations, damage groups, job types (a crew type, an action and a damage group, each with a duration and an effect on the network), and first- and second-order job priorities. Crews are assigned to jobs only if of the right type, idle, within zone when required, and with enough shift time left after travel; travel time is distance divided by a user-set speed, by default 18 km/h, and jobs that outlast a shift become long jobs. The tool was applied to a small test network and to the Los Angeles system for the January 17, 1994 Northridge earthquake and for 666 probabilistic earthquake damage scenarios; for Northridge the simulated water delivery and water quantity match the observed restoration within about 5% for most of the simulation and demand met within about 8%.
limits: A precedent for structure only: the crew, shift, travel and priority mechanisms model physical repair of earthquake-damaged pipes, tanks and pumps, and none of its durations, crew counts or priorities calibrate cyber recovery work. The validation errors are specific to the Los Angeles Northridge case, whose observed restoration was itself approximate, digitized years later, and shaped by improvised operational changes that the authors say a general model cannot predict. Local distribution networks are represented by demand nodes with no links to neighbouring networks.
